opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in a few layers. The most obvious one is the one everybody knows from the scaling laws: if you put more compute into pretraining, with more data and bigger models, you get steadily better models in a fairly predictable way. That predictability is part of what makes it so powerful. You can plan around it and make bets years in advance.

What's gotten really exciting more recently is that pretraining isn't the only place compute matters anymore. We've seen that you can scale compute at other stages too. Reinforcement learning is one. You let the model practice on hard problems, get feedback, and improve. Test-time compute is another. You let the model think longer before it answers. When a model can spend more time reasoning through a hard math problem or a tricky piece of code, it does meaningfully better. So now there are several knobs, not just one.

The way I like to frame it is that compute is a lever on the model's ability to learn and its ability to think. More compute in training means it learns more. More compute at inference means it can think more carefully about the specific problem in front of it. Those two compound each other.

I'd also say compute doesn't advance capabilities on its own. You need the right algorithms, the right data, and the right evaluations to know whether you're actually making progress on the things that matter. A lot of the craft is figuring out where the next unit of compute gives you the most return. Sometimes that's a bigger pretraining run. Sometimes it's better RL environments. Sometimes it's making inference cheaper so people can actually use the reasoning capabilities.

What I find most motivating is what this unlocks downstream. The capabilities themselves are interesting, but the real payoff is when they turn into things that help people: a scientist getting through experiments faster, a developer shipping something they couldn't have built alone, or someone getting a clearer answer to a medical question. That's what makes the investment in scaling feel worth it.

r001.rationale: It contrasts bigger models and more pretraining compute with additional inference-time compute for longer reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says larger pretraining runs produce steadily better models, but does not identify emergent capabilities.

r003.rationale: It describes letting a model think longer on hard problems, but does not say thinking time varies based on perceived difficulty.

r004.rationale: It says longer reasoning improves performance on hard problems, but does not state it enables previously inaccessible levels of difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I tend to think about scaling compute as having a few distinct levers rather than one dial, and it helps to keep them separate.

The first, and historically the most important, is pretraining compute. Bigger models trained on more data, with the right balance between parameters and tokens, learn richer representations of the world. What's remarkable is how predictable that has been: loss improves smoothly as a function of compute, and many downstream abilities ride along with it. That predictability is what let people make large bets with some confidence.

The second lever is what you might call post-training compute, especially reinforcement learning. Once a model has a good base of knowledge, spending compute on having it attempt hard problems, get feedback, and improve has turned out to be an unusually efficient use of resources. It's where a lot of reasoning capability has come from in the last couple of years, and the scaling curves there look much earlier on their trajectory than pretraining does.

The third is inference compute, giving the model more time to think at test time. That changed how I frame the whole question. It used to be that a model's capability was fixed at training time. Now there's a tradeoff surface: you can trade more thinking per query for better answers, and you can choose where on that surface to sit depending on the task. For something like a hard math proof or a multi-step coding task, letting the model search, verify, and backtrack is worth a lot.

Beyond those three, I'd mention two things that are easy to underrate. One is that compute buys you experiments. A lot of progress is not just the final big run, it's the hundreds of small runs that tell you which architecture, data mix, or training recipe to scale. Having the compute to iterate quickly compounds. The other is data generation. Models can now produce synthetic data, filter it, and verify it, and that's compute converting into training signal in a way that partly addresses the worry about running out of high-quality human text.

The caveats I take seriously are that scaling is necessary but not sufficient. The best algorithms shift the curve, and efficiency gains have been enormous, so raw FLOPs are not the whole story. Scaling also exposes bottlenecks elsewhere: evaluation gets harder, infrastructure gets harder, and the reliability and safety questions get more important as capabilities improve. So I'd say compute is the engine, but the direction you point it, and the care you take with what comes out, matter at least as much.

r001.rationale: It separates pretraining compute, including larger models, from inference compute that gives a model more time to think.

r002.rationale: It links bigger models to richer representations and says downstream abilities improve along with scaling.

r003.rationale: It says to choose how much thinking to spend depending on the task and gives hard problems as cases where more thinking helps.

r004.rationale: It says more thinking can improve answers on hard problems, but does not state that extra time lets models tackle difficulty levels that were previously inaccessible.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate two ways of scaling compute. One is during training: giving a model more compute to learn from data and develop capabilities. The other is at inference time: giving it more room to work through a problem before it answers—to explore different approaches, check its work, and revise a solution.

Those are complementary. Training can give you a stronger starting point, and inference-time compute can let you use that capability more effectively on a particular task. But more compute isn’t automatically more intelligence. You also need good learning methods, useful data, and ways to tell whether the model is actually making progress.

So the exciting question for me is: can we turn additional compute into reliably better answers, especially on problems where a quick response isn’t enough? And can we do that efficiently enough that those improvements are useful to people?

r001.rationale: It distinguishes training compute from inference-time compute, but does not identify increasing model size as the other scaling axis.

r002.rationale: It says training compute can develop capabilities, but does not state that increasing model size produces emergent capabilities.

r003.rationale: It describes giving a model more room to reason, but does not say the model varies its thinking time based on perceived problem difficulty.

r004.rationale: It says extra inference compute can help with problems that need more than a quick response, but does not claim this enables previously inaccessible levels of difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of compute as giving us more room to learn and more room to think. During training, more compute lets us explore larger models, more data, and longer training runs. At inference time, it can let a model spend more effort on a difficult problem—trying different approaches and checking its work before answering.

But compute isn’t the whole story. The training methods, the quality of the data, and how effectively the model uses that compute all matter. So the interesting question is both what happens when we scale up and how we make each unit of compute more useful.

Ultimately, I’d measure progress by what people can reliably do with the system. Does the additional compute help it solve harder problems, make fewer mistakes, and recognize when it doesn’t know? That’s what makes scaling valuable.

r001.rationale: It separately describes scaling training to explore larger models and using more compute at inference to spend extra effort on difficult problems.

r002.rationale: It mentions larger models but does not say that increasing model size produces emergent capabilities.

r003.rationale: It says a model can spend more effort on a difficult problem, linking inference effort to perceived problem difficulty.

r004.rationale: It says extra compute can help solve harder problems, but does not state that longer thinking makes previously inaccessible difficulty levels solvable.
